title: Morning Glory clouds
hook: A single cloud that can stretch for hundreds of kilometres and rolls like a wave.
peek: In northern Australia, spring mornings sometimes bring a tube of cloud that runs from horizon to horizon and rolls across the sky. Glider pilots travel there to ride it like surfers on a wave.
lede: Most clouds drift. The Morning Glory rolls. Over the Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia, usually between September and early November, a tube of cloud can appear at dawn that stretches for hundreds of kilometres. It tumbles forward like a rolling pin, often low over the ground, and the small town of Burketown has become its best-known viewing spot.

bullets.text: The leading explanation is that sea breezes from either side of the Cape York Peninsula meet overnight. The collision sets off a wave in the cool lower air, and the cloud forms along its crest as the air rises and cools.

Physicists treat the Morning Glory as a kind of solitary wave, a single hump of air that travels a long way without spreading out. The cloud marks where that hump lifts moist air high enough to condense.
It often comes as a set, with several rolls one behind another. As each passes overhead, people on the ground can feel a sudden gust and a jump in air pressure.
Glider pilots fly up the front of the cloud, where the air is rising, and can stay aloft for long stretches without an engine. Locals and visiting pilots treat the season as an informal pilgrimage.
